newsitem.title: FRANCE: French ambulances take protest to Eiffel Tower.
newsitem.headline: French ambulances take protest to Eiffel Tower.

text.p: Hundreds of ambulance drivers snarled traffic in central Paris for the second successive day on Friday in protest at cuts in social security payments hitting their business.
They camped in their vehicles under the Eiffel Tower overnight and later drove through the surrounding district at snail's pace as they waited to put forward their grievances at the Health Ministry.
The ministry, after receiving a group of the protesters, offered talks with Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot next week, possibly on Tuesday.
France's private ambulance drivers complain that new rules to limit the use of their vehicles to curb losses of the state welfare system will cut their business by up to a third.
Ambulance fees cost the welfare system an estimated six billion francs ($1.2 billion) a year. The drivers are paid by patients, who in turn are reimbursed partly by the state.
French ambulance companies employ about 40,000 people.

The government is striving to cut its budget deficit in line with Maastricht criteria to join the single European currency in 1999. It has launched wide-ranging reforms to try to restore financial health to the welfare system.

Under the new regulations, patients will be reimbursed ambulance fees only when they enter hospital and are discharged, and in some other limited cases. Fees were hitherto reimbursed for hospital visits up to three months after surgery.
